title: Mamie, szkole, pracy
title_en: Feminine nouns · one form for Dative and Locative
note:
B2 Block 1, unit 3. PAYS B1-DIGEST DEFERRED ITEM 1. b1_dative_sg handed mamie / tacie / siostrze over as memorised whole forms and logged: 'three different feminine consonant-softening classes (m->mi, t->ci, r->rz) plus brat's own irregular -u would be the do/z cliff again if derived honestly in one unit... The general feminine dative/locative rule stays untaught. James should decide whether it needs a slot.' B2-SPINE gave it this slot; this is that unit.

WHY IT IS LIGHT DESPITE LOOKING BIG: four of the nine forms drilled here are ALREADY IN THE POOL — mamie and siostrze as Datives (b1_dative_sg), szkole and pracy as Locatives (a1_prep_place / a1_prep_review_2). Only five forms are genuinely new: kobiecie, łazience, ulicy, kuchni, sypialni. So the unit is mostly revelation, not acquisition — the b2_verbal_nouns idiom of 'words you already say turn out to be one pattern'.

THE GIFT, and the reason this unit is worth its slot: for feminine nouns the Dative and the Locative are THE SAME FORM. It is exceptionless across every noun used here, and it means one rule pays for two cases. Slide 1 is entirely this, with three nouns shown doing both jobs side by side (Mówię o mamie / Pomagam mamie). The Genitive is also identical for the soft group (pracy, ulicy, kuchni) — named honestly in one explain string where the learner has already met do pracy, rather than left to look like a contradiction.

TWO CLASSES, and the one real judgment call in this unit:
- Class A, hard stem: -a -> -e, and the consonant before it softens. Five pairs shown as a visible family table (-ma->-mie, -ra->-rze, -ła->-le, -ta->-cie, -ka->-ce) with the slide saying outright that the learner is NOT expected to work these out for an unseen word — the closed-family treatment O10 prescribes and that kelnerzy / mógłby / the family datives already established.
- Class B, stem already soft: -y or -i instead, nothing else changing.
JUDGMENT CALL, logged: the conservative option was Class A only, deferring Class B. Rejected, because pracy is one of the most frequent forms in the whole course (w pracy, owned since A1) and would then sit in plain sight as a counterexample to the rule just taught. Teaching only half the split would actively mislead; the split itself costs one slide and no new alternation to memorise.

tata: named in ONE line on slide 2 and nowhere else. It is masculine but ends in -a and follows Class A, which is why the learner already says tacie (b1_dative_sg). tacie is already taught, so this adds no form and no rule — it exists only to stop the 'feminine' framing from un-teaching a word he owns. Deliberately not drilled: it appears in no match row, no quiz item, no type item, no use item.

FENCED: brat -> bratu and every masculine dative (b1_dative_sg owns -owi separately; this unit is about the -a class only). Feminine ACCUSATIVE forms (mamę, siostrę) appear only as wrong-slot quiz distractors, never taught or implied as part of this pattern. No plural anywhere — the plural obliques are their own three units later in B2. No new governors: every Locative frame uses w / na / o and every Dative frame uses pomagać / dziękować, all already owned.

DISTRACTORS are real taught forms in the wrong slot (the b1_imperative_rule convention), never fabricated: citation forms (kuchnia, łazienka, siostra, kobieta), already-taught accusatives (mamę, siostrę), the already-taught plural kobiety, and correct forms of the wrong noun. mamy was deliberately kept out of the distractor pool — AGENTS.md's own homograph table records it as the verb 'we have' (a1_miec), not a form of mama.

ONE PRESENTATION CHANGE made during self-verification, worth recording because it is the ci/ci trap arriving from an unexpected direction: slide 2's third column originally listed the alternations as bare consonant maps (m -> mi, t -> ci). Both mi and ci are already taught as DATIVE PRONOUNS (a2_dat_chunks, b1_dative_pron), and ci is the course's most documented two-meaning collision — printing it as a bare token inside a dative unit was asking for it to be read as the pronoun. Rewritten as whole ending-shapes (-ma -> -mie, -ta -> -cie), which is clearer for the learner anyway since it shows the actual shape of the word's end rather than an abstract letter map.

intro.title: One form, two jobs
intro.body: For feminine nouns, the form used after w, na and o is the same as the form used after pomagam and dziękuję. You have been using both for months without noticing: w szkole is one job, pomagam mamie is the other, and they are built the same way. Learn one form and you have both.

intro.title: How the form is made: -a comes off, -e goes on
intro.body: Take the -a off and put -e on. The consonant just before the ending changes as it goes. These are pairs to learn, not a sum to do — you are not expected to work out the right consonant for a word you have not seen before. One word here is not feminine at all: tata ends in -a and changes the same way, which is why you already say tacie.

intro.title: The second group: -y or -i, and nothing else changes
intro.body: Some feminine nouns already end in a soft consonant before the -a. There is nothing left to soften, so they simply take -y or -i and the stem stays as it is. This is why you have always said w pracy and never anything else.
intro.body_pl: w pracy · na ulicy · w kuchni · w sypialni

quiz.explain: kuchnia already ends in a soft consonant, so it takes -i and the stem stays as it is.
Same group as kuchnia — soft stem, so -i, nothing else changing.
łazienka is a hard stem, so it takes -e and the k softens to c: łazienka → łazience.
The same mamie you use in Mówię o mamie — one form doing both jobs. mamę is the form after mam, a different job again.
r → rz, exactly as in Myślę o siostrze. Learning it once covers both.
t → ci. And the same kobiecie works after pomagam: Pomagam kobiecie.
ł → l. You have said w szkole since the very first place lesson — this is the same form, now with o in front of it.
ulica is in the soft group with praca, so -y.
pomagam always takes this form of the noun. kobiety is the plural — more than one woman, and the wrong shape here anyway.
Myślę o siostrze is good Polish too, but it says "I'm thinking about my sister" — a different verb.
